title: This startup says it is not a new Bloomberg, but a recommendation system for traders
dek: The founder positions the company as a combination of Bloomberg, Claude, and Netflix: value lies not in giving traders more data, but in proactively surfacing second-order signals they wouldn't think to look for, like Netflix does.
why: Discusses a specific product idea (recommendation systems for financial terminals) and real-world noise in AI startup hiring; information density peaks mid-episode, with extended pleasantries up front.
who: Commodity and energy traders, buy-side alternative-data procurement, or AI engineers being asked to be one person doing one team's work.
skip: 22:00–23:30, conversation about conference organization logistics and personal grooming; unrelated to the product itself.

points.h: In four seconds, Moshi learns 300 new data points
points.body: The founder uses an analogy to illustrate the data density Moshi handles: this four-second sentence, she says, coincides with Moshi learning 300 new data points. Moshi is not another chatbot, but a real-time signal provider for commodity, energy, and macro traders—its goal is to deliver in 30 seconds a judgment that would otherwise take days to assemble, shifting the question of ‘which information matters’ from traders' heads into the system.

points.h: Not a new Bloomberg—a Netflix for traders
points.body: When asked if it is ‘a new Bloomberg,’ the founder clearly denies it, saying if Bloomberg, Claude, and Netflix had a child, that would be Moshi. The key difference lies in a homegrown recommendation system: when a trader is focused on one thing, the system knows they should care about second- and third-order relationships—for instance, how an energy company's moves indirectly affect oil prices. These signals won't appear in a news feed; they require an interconnected relationship graph to actively surface them.

points.h: Recommendation systems go ignored, yet are indispensable
points.body: The host notes that he hosts a dedicated recommendation-systems track at AI conferences each year, staffed by engineers who built YouTube, Netflix, Instagram, and TikTok's recommendation algorithms—yet the track is regularly empty. His explanation: recommendation systems are made to ‘look easy.’ Both agree further: anyone can now build their own Claude dashboard, but getting others to actually use it is a UI problem. Solve the recommendation system well, and the UI problem dissolves.

points.h: Twitter's Firehose costs $300,000 monthly and remains all noise
points.body: The host recalls that during his time at hedge fund Balyasny, it was among the earliest institutions to purchase X (Twitter) Firehose data, at roughly $300,000 monthly, yet data quality was poor—many post nonsense, and others deliberately manipulate markets. This exposes buyers' core concern: after paying for alternative data, they still may not dare trade on it directly.

points.h: Disagreement between Bloomberg, Reuters, and the Journal is itself a signal
points.body: Moshi's approach to noise is not to filter out uncertain information, but to display it with a confidence score. The founder illustrates: if Reuters, Bloomberg, and the Wall Street Journal disagree on how many ships or planes passed a location, that disagreement itself is a valuable data point—because nobody knows the truth, which precisely signals a potential trading opportunity.

points.h: Customer data stays in-house; self-built models follow
points.body: On whether to build a custom vision-language model to parse PDFs, the founder names two criteria: first, customer data doesn't go to third parties unless you can verify how they'll use it; second, if the team has engineering capacity—most Moshi staff have NASA backgrounds—building in-house is the better choice. But she acknowledges not every company has that option.

points.h: ‘You are the team’: engineers forced to do ten jobs solo
points.body: Among those who found the founder at the conference, beyond traders were many AI engineers, all describing pressure from management: ‘We don't need a team—you are the team.’ A system meant for ten people now falls to one. Worse, some build it only to find colleagues say they need it but never actually open it. The problem becomes non-adoption, not non-delivery.

points.h: One open role, four days, 2500 applications
points.body: On hiring versus sales priorities, the founder says finding customers is now the bottleneck, not hiring—one job posting draws 2500 applications in four days, forcing it to close. As a first-time founder, she admits not knowing at first how much noise saturates the pipeline: applicants using unauthorized work eligibility, for instance.
